How much mega backdoor Roth headroom do you have left this year?

If your 401(k) plan allows after-tax contributions above the ordinary deferral limit, this calculates the after-tax room you have left under the IRS's overall 415(c) limit for 2025 or 2026 -- and the per-paycheck amount to use all of it before year-end.

After using this, you can now see the exact dollar headroom left in your plan's after-tax bucket this year, the per-paycheck contribution that reaches it by December, and whether your own plan's contribution cap (not just the IRS limit) is what's actually binding. See how conversion frequency changes what you owe or what a hand estimate usually gets wrong.

Your numbers

Everything below is what you already have on your latest paystub or plan portal for this employer's plan. Nothing is uploaded -- the calculation runs entirely in this browser.

Optional: your plan's own after-tax cap (if it has one below the IRS limit)
Optional: estimate the tax cost of a delayed conversion

Max additional after-tax you can contribute this year:

    Everything you enter stays on this device. Nothing is uploaded. Usage counts contain only feature names and are never sent anywhere.

    Common questions

    What is the mega backdoor Roth 401(k) strategy?

    Some 401(k) plans let you contribute after-tax dollars beyond the ordinary employee deferral limit, up to a much larger IRS ceiling that also covers your employer's contributions. Converting that after-tax money to Roth -- through an in-plan Roth conversion or an in-service withdrawal to a Roth IRA -- moves it into Roth tax treatment: no tax on qualified withdrawals in retirement. Most plans do not offer this; check your plan document or ask your plan administrator before assuming it applies to you.

    What's the difference between the $24,500 limit and the $72,000-$83,250 limit?

    The $23,500 (2025) / $24,500 (2026) figure is the 402(g) elective deferral limit -- what you control directly through payroll withholding, pre-tax plus Roth 401(k) combined. The much larger $70,000-$81,250 (2025) / $72,000-$83,250 (2026) figure is the 415(c) overall limit -- your elective deferral, your employer's match and profit sharing, and any after-tax contributions, all added together. The gap between what you and your employer have already put in under the smaller limit and the larger limit is your after-tax headroom.

    If I changed jobs this year, does the 415(c) limit combine across both employers?

    No, and this is the opposite of how the other limit works. The 415(c) overall limit applies per employer plan (or per controlled group of related employers) -- a job change generally gives you a fresh 415(c) ceiling at the new employer. The 402(g) elective deferral limit is the reverse: it is one shared ceiling across every employer you contributed to during the calendar year, related or not, so your pre-tax and Roth paycheck deferrals at both jobs combined still cannot exceed it. This calculator computes the 415(c) headroom for a single employer's plan; if you changed jobs, run it once per employer with each plan's own YTD figures.

    Why does converting quickly matter more than converting eventually?

    After-tax contributions themselves are not taxed again on withdrawal or conversion -- you already paid tax on that money once. Any investment growth on that after-tax balance before you convert it, though, is taxed as ordinary income at conversion. A plan with automatic or same-day in-plan Roth conversion leaves little or no growth to accumulate, so the conversion is close to tax-free. A plan that only lets you convert periodically (quarterly, annually) lets growth build up in the after-tax bucket first, and that growth is what gets taxed when you finally convert. See the full comparison.

    Is this the same as a regular backdoor Roth IRA?

    No, and the two get confused constantly. A backdoor Roth IRA is a nondeductible contribution to a traditional IRA (capped at $7,000 for 2025/2026, plus a $1,000 catch-up at 50+) that you then convert to a Roth IRA -- and it can trigger the IRA pro-rata rule if you hold other pre-tax IRA money. The mega backdoor Roth happens entirely inside your 401(k), uses the much larger 415(c) limit instead of the IRA limit, and has no IRA pro-rata-rule exposure at all.

    Does my plan have to offer this?

    Yes -- and most plans do not. Three separate plan features all have to be present: the plan must allow after-tax (non-Roth) employee contributions above the elective-deferral limit, and it must allow either in-plan Roth conversions or in-service withdrawals so the after-tax money can actually move to Roth. Some plans that allow after-tax contributions still lock the money up until termination, which removes most of the benefit. Check your plan's summary plan description or ask your plan administrator before assuming any of this applies to you.

This tool does not know whether your specific plan allows after-tax contributions, in-plan Roth conversions, or in-service withdrawals -- confirm all three with your plan document or administrator before contributing a dollar based on this page. vs-doing-the-math-by-hand.html.text:

This calculator vs. working out your headroom by hand

The arithmetic behind mega backdoor Roth headroom is not hard once every input is right. What goes wrong in a spreadsheet or a mental estimate is almost always one of two omissions, and both push the estimate the same direction: they make it look like there is more room than the plan will actually allow.

A worked example

A saver turning 61 this year, with $12,000 already withheld from their own paycheck, a $6,000 employer match and profit-sharing contribution so far, another $6,000 of employer money expected before year-end, and no after-tax contributions yet.

StepTypical by-hand estimateWhat this calculator does
Which limit appliesAnchors to the $24,500 figure everyone has seen in headlines, and treats that as the ceiling for after-tax room tooUses the 2026 overall 415(c) limit ($72,000 base), not the smaller 402(g) elective-deferral limit -- the two are different numbers for a different purpose
Catch-up amountApplies the standard 50+ catch-up ($8,000 for 2026) because that is the number most articles quoteRecognizes age 61 falls in the SECURE 2.0 enhanced catch-up band (60-63) and applies $11,250 instead, for an $83,250 ceiling rather than $80,000
What already counts against itSubtracts only the after-tax dollars contributed so far ($0), leaving an apparent $83,250 of headroomNets out the elective deferral already withheld ($12,000) and every employer dollar already deposited or still expected ($12,000), for real headroom of $59,250
ResultOverstates headroom by $24,000 -- the exact amount of the employer money the estimate forgot to countReports the figure the plan will actually honor, plus the per-paycheck amount to use it up by year-end

Figures use the 2026 limits this calculator ships with; see the calculator for the 2025 figures.

Common questions

What's the most common mistake in a by-hand estimate?

Subtracting only the after-tax dollars already contributed from the big 415(c) number, and forgetting that the elective deferral and every employer match or profit-sharing dollar deposited this year also count against that same ceiling. That single omission overstates headroom by whatever the employer has already put in — often several thousand dollars — and the saver finds out only when the plan rejects a contribution or, worse, does not and creates an excess annual addition.

Why does the catch-up amount trip up a manual estimate specifically?

SECURE 2.0 gives savers who turn 60, 61, 62, or 63 during the year a larger "enhanced" catch-up than everyone else 50 and older gets. A spreadsheet built once and reused every year, or copied from a generic article about the standard catch-up, applies the smaller number to someone in that four-year band and understates their real ceiling — leaving real tax-advantaged room unused, which cannot be made up after December 31.

How does mixing up the two limits happen?

The $23,500 (2025) / $24,500 (2026) figure everyone quotes is the 402(g) elective deferral limit — your own payroll withholding. The after-tax headroom this strategy uses comes from the much larger 415(c) overall limit, $70,000-$81,250 (2025) or $72,000-$83,250 (2026) depending on age. An estimate that anchors to the smaller, more famous number treats most of the real headroom as if it did not exist.

Does a spreadsheet formula fix this?

Only if it is rebuilt correctly every year with that year's IRS figures, the saver's exact catch-up band, every dollar already contributed by both the saver and the employer at this specific employer's plan, and the plan's own after-tax cap if it has one below the IRS ceiling. A formula copied from a prior year, or from a generic template that does not separate 402(g) from 415(c), reproduces the same mistakes a purely mental estimate makes — it is just wrong with more decimal places.

What does this calculator do differently?

It applies the correct year's IRS figures and age-adjusted catch-up automatically, nets every dollar already counted — elective deferral, employer match and profit sharing, and after-tax contributions already made — against the 415(c) ceiling, and separately checks the plan's own after-tax percentage cap when one is entered, reporting whichever of the two actually binds. Nothing is uploaded; it runs the same arithmetic a correct spreadsheet would, without the two steps a hand estimate most often skips.

This page names no specific plan provider, spreadsheet, or competing product — it compares this calculator against estimating the same arithmetic yourself, not against another tool.

which-conversion-cadence-should-i-use.ht.text:
← back to the calculator

Which Roth conversion cadence should I use?

Your after-tax 401(k) contribution was already taxed once, so converting it to Roth triggers no additional tax on the contribution itself. The investment growth that happens between contributing and converting is different: it is taxed as ordinary income the year you convert. Cadence is entirely about how much growth accumulates before that happens.

The three paths, compared

PathGrowth exposed to taxWho controls it after
Automatic / same-day in-plan conversionClose to zero — typically a day or two of growth per contributionStays in the 401(k) as a Roth 401(k) source, your plan's investment menu
Periodic in-plan conversion (quarterly/annual)Whatever the after-tax balance earned since the last conversionStays in the 401(k) as a Roth 401(k) source
In-service withdrawal to a Roth IRAWhatever the after-tax balance earned before the withdrawal, same as periodic conversion if not done immediatelyMoves to a Roth IRA you control directly, with its own investment options

Common questions

Why does conversion cadence matter at all?

Your after-tax 401(k) contribution was already taxed once when you earned it, so converting the contribution itself to Roth triggers no additional tax. Any investment growth on that money between the contribution and the conversion is a different story: it is taxed as ordinary income in the year you convert. The longer the gap between contributing and converting, the more growth accumulates, and the larger that tax bill gets.

What does automatic or same-day conversion do?

Some plan providers convert each after-tax contribution to Roth automatically, often within the plan's own processing window (commonly next business day). With growth measured in a day or two rather than a quarter or a year, the taxable amount is close to zero on every conversion. This is the cleanest version of the strategy and the one most write-ups assume, but it requires your specific plan and recordkeeper to actually support it -- many do not.

What does periodic or manual conversion cost that automatic conversion does not?

If you convert quarterly, annually, or only when you remember to, the after-tax bucket sits invested for that whole period first. Whatever it earns in that time is ordinary taxable income at conversion -- not capital-gains-rate income, and not tax-free. A saver contributing early in the year and converting only at year-end effectively volunteers for a year of market growth to be taxed at their marginal rate instead of eventually being Roth-tax-free growth.

Is an in-service withdrawal to a Roth IRA different from an in-plan conversion?

Both move after-tax 401(k) money (and its growth) into Roth treatment, and both tax the growth portion the same way. The practical difference is destination and control: an in-plan conversion stays inside the 401(k) as a separate Roth 401(k) source, subject to the plan's own investment menu and rules; an in-service withdrawal moves the money out to a Roth IRA you control directly, with the IRA's own investment options and withdrawal rules (including the five-year rule on converted amounts). Not every plan allows either one -- some allow after-tax contributions but neither conversion path, which removes most of the strategy's benefit.

How do I find out what my own plan actually allows?

Your plan's summary plan description (SPD) is the authoritative source, or a direct question to your plan administrator or HR/benefits contact: does the plan allow after-tax (non-Roth) employee contributions above the elective-deferral limit, and does it offer in-plan Roth conversion or in-service withdrawals, and if so how often. This calculator cannot know your plan's specific rules -- it only computes the dollar headroom once you know whether the strategy is available to you at all.

This page names no specific plan provider or product -- it compares the generic conversion mechanisms available across 401(k) plans in general, not a competing tool.
